Page 1, the cover: GEMS-TAIWAN · iGEM 2026 · ReLEAF Hardware Notebook Week by week, 23 March to 17 October 2026 WHAT THIS IS A record of the hardware we built for ReLEAF, one week at a time. Nine things got made: a humidity box, an agar plate…
Page 2, the contents: weeks 4 to 22, one row per entry with its week, title, build and number
Page 3, the contents, continued: weeks 22 to 33, one row per entry with its week, title, build and number

Page 4, week 4, Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen: Our first plan was a sealed growth chamber with hydroponics inside it. Arabidopsis needs steady humidity, temperature and light to give comparable results, and the school lab could not hold any of those steady. The chamber was…

Page 5, Sourcing finished, purchasing frozen, continued: DECISION Freeze purchasing instead of building in parallel If half of it was already built we’d have argued to keep going. We hadn’t spent anything yet, so stopping was free. REJECTED Ordering the slow-delivery parts anyway to…

Page 6, week 5, Visiting Prof. Verslues: We had a chamber design nobody had agreed to and a purchasing freeze. None of us had seen a working plant growth setup, so we went to look at one before designing any more of our own. Incubator shelf with vertical agar plates…

Page 7, week 6, Told to drop soil sensing: Our original plan was to sense drought stress in soil and release protectant into the soil directly. Before committing to it we wanted someone who sells into agriculture to tell us whether it held up. Meeting in progress…

Page 8, week 7, The pivot, and asking Dr. Pak where to start: This is the week the project changed shape. The pivot document went up on 15 April: instead of sensing soil and releasing into it, engineered B. subtilis would live inside a sealed vessel, and light would tell them when to…

Page 9, week 8, Working out what a stress assay should measure: The pivot had landed but the plant side of the project had no experiment behind it. Before building anything for the plants we needed to agree what stress we would apply, at what level, and what we would measure to say whether…

Page 10, week 9, Nothing much happened: only the productive weeks misrepresents how the summer actually went. pre WEEK 09 27 APRIL – 3 MAY 2026 A quiet week. Several of us were away. Kept in the record because a notebook containing PROBLEMS HOW WE’LL FIX IT A week lost…

Page 11, week 10, Four instruments, three people: The instructors asked for a milestone and a deadline against every task in the project. Writing the list turned out to be more useful than the list itself. 9 May: the hydroponic prototype set up for the wet lab, the one piece of…

Page 12, week 11, Dropping the fluorometer: The chlorophyll fluorometer would have let us measure plant stress directly, by reading damage to photosystem II. Fv/Fm is the standard number for that, and a healthy plant sits around 0.78 to 0.83. It was the fourth instrument…

Page 13, Dropping the fluorometer, continued: 16 May: bioreactor layout A sketched the same day 16 May: layout B DECISION Drop the fluorometer on capacity, not feasibility The science holds up. It was never a feasibility problem, only a staffing one. Better to finish two…

Page 14, week 12, Humidity box finished, agar photos useless: The humidity box is a small sealed enclosure that keeps humidity steady while Arabidopsis germinates. It came out of the Verslues visit and it is the first thing we finished. The same week we started growing on agar plates, and…

Page 15, week 13, Building the agar plate imaging station: The imaging station is a rig that holds a phone in a fixed position over an agar plate, under fixed lighting, so photos taken days apart can be compared. It is the answer to the problem from last week. The light ring lit inside…

Page 16, Building the agar plate imaging station, continued: DECISION Ridges to take the tension out, and a slide-in slot Creasing at the ridges is predictable. Left alone the strip buckles wherever it wants. With a slot we can replace the strip without reprinting the ring. REJECTED Gluing…

Page 17, week 13, Assembly guide tested by handing it over: The light plate apparatus (LPA, called DiOPAL until October) shines green and red light into wells of bacteria. Green switches the CcaS-CcaR circuit on and red switches it off, so the plate is how we control when the bacteria…

Page 18, Assembly guide tested by handing it over, continued: TABLE 8 Part Spec Note Plate 24-well, 3D printed lid does not seat LEDs 520 nm green, 660 nm red first row only MCU Arduino Uno breadboarded, not soldered Guide LPA_Assembly_Guide_v2.docx step level, 20+ steps Parts as actually…

Page 19, week 14, Bioreactor prototype I built: The bioreactor is the vessel the pivot committed us to. Bacteria live inside a hollow fibre membrane while the protectant they make crosses the membrane and leaves, which keeps the organism contained. Prototype I is the simplest…

Page 20, Bioreactor prototype I built, continued: 1 June: light plate, first light in both colours TABLE 9 Component Spec Note Membrane PES hollow fibre lumen ~200 mL Reservoir 500 mL bottle, 300 mL LB no stirring Pump peristaltic target 94 mL/min Sampling luer valve on the…

Page 21, week 15, The cells barely grow in the reactor: This is the first run of prototype I. We grew the same culture in the reactor and in a flask at the same time, both at room temperature, so the flask acts as a control. If the reactor works, the two curves should look alike.…

Page 22, The cells barely grow in the reactor, continued: Shell-side plate, no colonies 13 June: the loop redrawn for prototype II after this run CANDIDATE CAUSES · TABLE 10 Candidate cause How we would tell it apart Status No active mixing, cells settle Add a stirrer and repeat. to…

Page 23, week 15, Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours: Prototype I barely grew and we had four candidate reasons. Prototype II changes three of them at once, which is not how you isolate a cause, but we had weeks, not months. 14 June: sampling the reactor arm Sampling the flask arm…

Page 24, Prototype II reaches plateau in two hours, continued: The DBTL summary slide we made for prototype II DECISION Passed. Faster to plateau and higher than the control Faster to plateau and higher at plateau than the control, which is more than we expected. Whether stirring alone would…

Page 25, week 16, Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design: Prof. Chang (張嘉修) is a chair professor in chemical engineering at NCKU who has published on B. subtilis bioreactor systems, so he was the right person to show the design to. He found a hole in it that none of us had seen. 18…

Page 26, Prof. Chang finds the gap in the design, continued: Group photo after the meeting 17 June: the roadmap redrawn around his points DECISION Add a valve after the membrane A valve after the membrane is the mechanism we were missing entirely. Hydroponics as the delivery target, which…

Page 27, week 16, Wrong unit for the light dose: The CcaS-CcaR circuit responds to a specific photon flux, so the light dose the plate delivers has to be a known quantity. This week we found we had been about to measure it in entirely the wrong unit. TABLE 12a Quantity Value…

Page 28, week 16, Temperature sensor driving the green channel: The whole project is one sentence: sense stress, emit light, release protectant. This is the first time the sensing end and the light end ran together on a bench, two months after the pivot. demo Wired an SHT31 temperature and…

Page 29, week 17, Making the plate float: Arabidopsis grows hydroponically on a plate sitting over liquid medium. The roots have to reach the liquid without the plate flooding, and our first version was fixed in place, which meant setting the level by hand every day and…

Page 30, Making the plate float, continued: Prototype 3 in CAD, cut through the seed holders: sealed chambers in violet Prototype 3 printed parts: plate, two clip-in handles, thirteen seed holders DECISION Float the platform instead of controlling the level The height…

Page 31, week 18, Iteration 1. Bubbles and drift: The photometer measures how much B. subtilis is in the reactor loop without taking samples out. An amber LED shines through a thin flow cuvette and we read how much light gets through. A beamsplitter sends part of the beam to a…

Page 32, Iteration 1. Bubbles and drift, continued: DECISION Move the cuvette to the base Bubbles rise, so putting the cuvette at the bottom takes them out of the beam without us doing anything. A dual luer valve and syringes let us pull the gas out on demand. Mounting vertically…

Page 33, week 18, Iteration 2. Zeroed against the wrong thing: Iteration 1 drifted and bubbled. Iteration 2 moves the cuvette to the base, turns the whole assembly upright and tightens every mount. This is the first time we tested against a sample where we already knew the answer. Iteration…

Page 34, Iteration 2. Zeroed against the wrong thing, continued: DECISION Did not pass. The procedure was wrong, not the optics We zeroed against the medium instead of clear water, so the zero was wrong from the start. Everything after a bad blank carries that error, no matter how good the…

Page 35, week 18, Rewriting the spec, and pulling a claim: Bioreactor parts had been discussed across four Discord channels and several documents, and the numbers had drifted apart from each other. This week we wrote one specification and checked every line of it against the parts we had…

Page 36, week 19, Iteration 3. Response does not double: Iteration 2 was zeroed against the wrong reference, so its numbers meant nothing. Iteration 3 fixes the procedure, tilts the stand so bubbles clear, and this time reads two concentrations instead of one so we can see whether the…

Page 37, Iteration 3. Response does not double, continued: Wiring at the sensor end DECISION Procedure fixed, but the response does not scale Blanking on water gives us a zero we can defend. CONFIDENCE Absolute lux dropped hard between iterations, 660 to 137. Something changed in the LED…

Page 38, week 19, Transmembrane pressure on a screen: A hollow fibre membrane fouls as it runs, and fouling shows up as pressure building across the membrane. Until this week we had no way of seeing that happen, so we could not tell a clean run from a blocked one. 10 July…

Page 39, week 20, LPA V3 finished: Prototype 1 of the light plate lit one row back on 1 June. Milestone 2 asked for tunable intensity in both colours across the whole array. This is the packaged version, V3. 17 July: printed parts arrived, first full assembly From…

Page 40, week 20, Measuring every LED before wiring: The intensity tiers on the light plate only mean something if the LEDs inside a tier actually match each other. Before wiring V3 we measured every LED we had bought, one at a time. The printed jig: one LED lit at the centre, lux…

Page 41, Measuring every LED before wiring, continued: Sorting into matched sets The sorted LEDs laid out before rewiring DECISION Passed. Matched sets hold the tiers apart Spread inside each tier after sorting is much smaller than the spread we started with. CONFIDENCE We…

Page 42, week 20, Reading four times high on the reactor: Iteration 4 is the final photometer build, with the component positions fixed, TPU-lined mounts so the glass is not scratched, and snap-in covers along the light path to block room light. This is the first time it went onto the…

Page 43, Reading four times high on the reactor, continued: TABLE 20 Trial Ours BioDrop Ours / BioDrop Before patch not recorded 0.149 approx 4× After patch 0.100 0.149 0.67× 18 July: the same week, the hollow-fibre set-ups we studied at BIO Asia–Taiwan DECISION Did not pass, but we know…

Page 44, week 21, Starting the nineteen-day run: We had checked the photometer against a benchtop reading once, with someone watching. What we did not know was whether it holds up over days on its own. The reactor was running anyway, so we logged the whole thing from 21 July.…

Page 45, Starting the nineteen-day run, continued: TABLE 21 Reading at 1 d Value Designed Note Points logged 291 — ~1 per 8.9 min Sample channel 195.54 lux — — Reference channel 28.47 lux — — Sample : reference 7.33× 10× unexplained Bubble reject rate 0 % — rule undocumented…

Page 46, week 22, The photometer catches the pump failing: The run had been going since 21 July and the curve was not the shape any of us expected. We spent most of the week arguing about why, then on 1 August it dropped and stayed down. SYMPTOM Nineteen days of continuous logging. No…

Page 47, The photometer catches the pump failing, continued: CANDIDATE CAUSES · TABLE 22 Candidate cause How we would tell it apart Status Recirculation pump failed Inspect the pump. If dead, replace and watch the trace. confirmed Contamination by another organism Plate a sample and look…

Page 48, week 22, Plotting the 434-hour trace with 1 August marked: Entry 22 ended with an action we never closed: plot the long run with the pump failure annotated. This is that plot, made from the raw log (0721, test3 20 day.csv: 2,720 rows, 434.2 hours, 21 July to 8 August). It does not look…

Page 49, Plotting the 434-hour trace with 1 August marked, continued: DECISION Report the late part of the run as a sensor failure, not as biology The reference beam never touches the culture, so its collapse is the instrument. Entry 22’s pump failure is still the confirmed event on the bench. What…

Page 50, week 23, Decision matrix: pinch valve actuator: Prof. Chang told us in June we had no way to push protectant out of the membrane, so we built a stepper pinch valve. This week we replaced it, on criteria written before we scored anything. 7 August: testing the printed valve…

Page 51, week 23, Assembling the full rig: The valve, the sensors and the photometer had all been built separately. This is the week the whole thing went together as one machine. 4 August: the perfusion set-up as drawn for the wiki 8 August: the rig set up with the green…

Page 52, Assembling the full rig, continued: 8 August: the hardware and bioreactor members with an instructor in front of the rig DECISION Photometer downstream of the pump The pump puts a sawtooth into the flow. We saw it in the pressure trace on 12 July. Putting the beam…

Page 53, week 23, Rewiring the light plate after it stopped lighting: The packaged LPA had been sitting since July without running a culture. When we came back to it on 7 August, part of the array did not light. This entry was added on 17 October from the photographs and the photo bank; nobody…

Page 54, week 24, Where the bioreactor stood on 13 August: This was the last week the first edition of this notebook covered, and the bioreactor was part way through a rebuild with three problems open, all of them mechanical. We had expected the biology to be the hard part. 5 August…

Page 55, Where the bioreactor stood on 13 August, continued: 11 August: changing the hardware CAD on the visit to the 源鮮 hydroponic farm DECISION Design around the weak pump instead of reverting Arduino control is the difference between automated and somebody standing there. The…

Page 56, week 24, Pressure on the new membrane, and the magnetic pump fails its first job: A new hollow fibre module arrived and had to be wetted and pressure-checked before any culture went into it. The same week the magnetic pump from entry 24 met the loop for the first time. 13 August: pressure-transducer test on…

Page 57, Pressure on the new membrane, and the magnetic pump fails its first job, continued: DECISION Stay on the peristaltic pump The magnetic pump cannot drive the loop, and a reactor that cannot circulate is worse than one that needs a person nearby. On 4 September Joshua confirmed the rig runs a peristaltic pump…

Page 58, week 25, Pressure drop against flow rate: We could read pressure (entry 17) but did not know what pressure the module should show at a given flow. Without that baseline, a rise from fouling and a rise from simply pumping faster look the same. Pass condition: measured…

Page 59, week 25, Rebuilding the reactor inside a computer case: The rig had grown across a bench: reservoir, pump, membrane, photometer, board and laptop, all loose. A farmer cannot be handed that. On 23 August we started moving it into a PC case, using water-cooling parts as the frame for…

Page 60, Rebuilding the reactor inside a computer case, continued: 22 August: whiteboard session on the bioreactor before the rebuild The case at the end of the first day DECISION Package the reactor in a PC case It turns a bench of loose parts into one object a farmer could be handed.…

Page 61, week 25, Calibrating against weighed titanium dioxide: Entries 16 and 20 left two open problems: we did not know if the response was linear, and we had one paired reading against the BioDrop. A growing culture changes while it is measured, so we needed an inert standard added in…

Page 62, Calibrating against weighed titanium dioxide, continued: DECISION Passed. No correction transform applied 3.8 % median difference against a 10 % target, with no calibration fitted. Fitting our readings to the BioDrop would only tie them to the BioDrop’s own error. CONFIDENCE Neither…

Page 63, week 26, Not ready for the forum: The Green Media forum on 5 September was the first time the cased reactor would be shown in public. On 30 August, six days out, Timmy listed what was missing. 29 August: routing tubing in the case Cutting tubing to length Fitting…

Page 64, week 27, First integrated run: the protectant crosses the membrane: Every piece had been tested alone. This run put the culture, pump, membrane, photometer and pressure logging together with a strain that secretes ACC deaminase all the time (constitutive), so light control was outside the test.…

Page 65, First integrated run: the protectant crosses the membrane, continued: Western blot: lumen lysate, lumen medium and shell medium, 14–44 h, ACC deaminase marked at ~42 kDa DECISION Passed, weakly. ACC deaminase reaches the shell side A band where it should be, on the side of the membrane the product…

Page 66, week 27, The cased reactor in front of the public: On 5 September the cased reactor went to the Green Media forum booth as a display: pump, green LED strip and screen running, sensors not wired, as agreed in entry 26. 5 September: looking into the case The green light through the…

Page 67, week 28, Drawing the rig as built, and why every transducer gets a filter: Jacquelyn was drawing the bioreactor for the wiki and the 12 September meeting with Prof. Sattely and Prof. Endy, and kept finding that no drawing matched the rig. On 11 September Chars drew it by hand, coloured by status. 11…

Page 68, Drawing the rig as built, and why every transducer gets a filter, continued: Prototype 4 as drawn on 14 September 15 September: the two final fixes, marked DECISION A Luer valve and a filter on every transducer Without them a transducer cannot be calibrated, and an uncalibrated reading is what the 4…

Page 69, week 29, A cheaper photometer: fibres in place of the lens and beam splitter: The beam splitter, the paralleling lens and the flow cuvette are nearly all of the complex photometer’s cost. Optical fibres can carry the light in parallel and split it 1:1 between sample and reference, which removes the lens…

Page 70, week 29, First culture under the light plate, and the post snaps on the shaker: The LPA had lit LEDs since May and never a culture. On 19 September it ran the first one, ACC deaminase level 2, with twelve tubes across green and red at three intensities. SYMPTOM Overnight on a shaker, a bottom-plate post…

Page 71, week 30, Black holder, four screws, MOSFETs inside: The rebuild after entry 30. The record gives no date for it, only that it came after the shaker failure and before the wiki’s final design in October. Before: three MOSFETs on a breadboard beside the holder After: perfboard and…

Page 72, Black holder, four screws, MOSFETs inside, continued: DECISION Fix the leak and the base in one rebuild Both failures came from the same run and both are print and assembly changes. CONFIDENCE The rebuilt base has not been back on a shaker, and no culture has run under the final…

Page 73, week 30, Soldering the valve power system: Prototype 2 adds control: servo pinch valves at the membrane and pH dosing. On 26 September Joshua’s goal was to finish soldering the power system (電壓系統). 26 September: the soldering bench The driver board Valve wiring laid out…

Page 74, week 31, Registering a growth-rate forecast before the run: A model that is only ever checked against data it has already seen proves little. On 1 October, before any bioreactor run of WB800 secreting ACC deaminase, we registered what the next run’s growth rate would be, with a pass…

Page 75, week 32, Run 5: the reading breaks down after ten hours: On 8 October we began the second full run through the bioreactor, with WB800 secreting codon-optimised ACC deaminase constitutively, at 37 °C, permeate drawn at 24 mL/min (a flux of 72 LMH). It was the first run that could score…

Page 76, Run 5: the reading breaks down after ten hours, continued: CANDIDATE CAUSES · TABLE 33 What the log shows What it means Status A sixth of windows carried more than 20 % bubbles bubbles in the beam confirmed in the log Reference channel moved 4.8× across the run the optics, not the…

Page 77, week 32, Silica calibration: both photometers on one series: TiO₂ (entry 25b) stopped at OD600 1.9 and never included the simplified photometer. On 10 October we ran silica, the iGEM standard, through the same loop with the BioDrop, the complex photometer and the simplified photometer…

Page 78, Silica calibration: both photometers on one series, continued: Timmy #📐-drylab · 11 October V1 more sheer light intensity, but shaky when OD gets high. V2 lower light intensity, but more stable, and less sensitivity so might miss small turbulence. 12 October: the newer photometer, light…

Page 79, week 32, Modelling the lab bioreactor as it is plumbed: The wiki needed a model of the lab bioreactor that matched the rig, not the September drawings. Anton revised the rack model and asked Chars to check it on 9 October. 9 October: the revised rack model Front elevation with labels…

Page 80, week 33, Run 6: a clean curve, and the forecast passes: Same strain as run 5, with two changes: permeate halved to 12 mL/min (36 LMH) and the photometer acceptance gate running. Pass condition, registered on 1 October: fitted growth rate inside 0.2705 to 0.3300 h⁻¹. sample beam lost…

Page 81, Run 6: a clean curve, and the forecast passes, continued: DECISION Passed on the one scored endpoint The rate fitted to run 6 sits inside the interval registered thirteen days before it. CONFIDENCE Over those five hours a straight line fits the readings with half the residual sum of…

Page 82, week 33, Auditing the parts list, and finding the pressure scaling wrong: The hardware material list of 7 October was complete but unpublishable: eleven internal contradictions, two of them live on the wiki. On 14 October the instructors ruled on each, the same exercise as the spec freeze of 4 July…
